explanation: No clear shared feature: fires on fragments inside proper names and rare words (place names, surnames, Velcro, Versailles), on ' a' in 'X is a village in', on technical adjectives (vertical, wide, temporal), and on code/LaTeX syntax tokens. The best guess is mid-word or mid-name tokens in unusual or foreign words, but this does not explain many of the examples.

Fires on the second token of a fixed multi-word expression or compound, where the previous token strongly predicts it (full width, short answer, foreign key, Coma Scale, let's face, lucky enough, If applicable, Washington University, [@pone). Strength depends on how conventional the collocation is. Ordinary function words fire weakly.

Fires on a unit-of-measure token right after a number, strongest for mass and amount units in concentrations and doses (mg, µg, g, nmol, mol, ng, mL, often followed by /kg or /L). Time, length and currency units after numbers fire moderately, and bare digits or exponents only weakly.

Fires on tokens in non-English Romance and Germanic text (Portuguese, Spanish, French, German), especially function words like que, se, você, onde, für and word-internal pieces. It also fires on name fragments and all-caps legal text in English. Plain English prose fires weakly or not at all.

Fires on the subword 'lig'/'olig' in oligo- words (oligosaccharide, Oligolepis, oligomer, oligarchy) and in oblig- words. It fires moderately on '-lation' in 'ablation' and on similar fragments after 'ol'/'ab' (olfactory, occlusion). The trigger is the spelling fragment, not the meaning.

Heterogeneous: fires on R Shiny 'ui'/'shinyUI', 'Program Files' in Windows paths, the '.' in legal citations 'So.2d', license-boilerplate words (FOR, LIABLE), and various content words in technical prose (control, propulsion, in vivo, compete). No single context explains it.

Fires mostly on tokens inside source code: generic type parameters (T1, T), format specifiers (%d), identifier pieces, punctuation in config and JSON, and version-year digits in copyright headers. It also fires on scattered prose tokens (and, event, able, occurred). The core is code-syntax tokens, with substantial noise from prose.

Mixture: 'of'/'nearest' in templated math questions ('prime factors of', 'Round to the nearest'), 'cell' in 'squamous cell', version digits in license strings (3.0), 'import (' in Go, 'at' in stack traces, and assorted name fragments. These look like positions inside highly formulaic boilerplate text, but the members are unrelated.

Its strongest examples are about periodicity, rotation and astronomy (Earth's tilt, periodic extension, 2π, heliospheric). It also fires moderately on numbers and spaces in timestamps, equations and CSS values (the seconds digit in times, the space before a number after '='). The examples look like two loosely linked jobs: cyclic/periodic concepts and numeric time/equation formatting.

Fires on the token right after a sentence or clause opener in templated math problems ('Suppose -', '. Let', 'Solve -'), and on negations or modals in English (n't, not, can, possible). It also fires on some Chinese tokens. Most cases are the slot just before a predicate or a negative sign, but the set is mixed.

Fires mainly on 'and' joining the last item of a coordinated pair or list ('students and subjects', 'radiotherapy and chemotherapy', 'X, Y and Z'). It also fires on fragments inside foreign proper names and species names (Radviliškis, Kotaku, formosanus). The coordination use is the dominant one.

Fires on a month name or season word in a date or time expression, especially right after a dateline, byline or 'in' (July 23, June 9, in January, the summer of). It also fires on some other words that start a named phrase (Yellow Sea, Nuevo México, Turbo C++). Month tokens in dates fire most reliably.

Fires on content words from health, nutrition and pharmacology (calorie, allergy, energy balance, maintenance, resistance, agar, drug fragments like fluorouracil and Stanozolol). It also picks up a few compound heads outside that domain (social security, Short-Term Memory). This is a broad biomedical/diet vocabulary unit.

Fires on word-internal subword pieces of words split into unusual tokens, especially in non-English text (Portuguese, French, German, Japanese/Hindi byte fragments), on garbled or mojibake bytes, and on odd splits in English (anticonvulsant, unspecific, endotracheal). It responds to the token being a mid-word fragment, not to any meaning.
